<!--

We close this part of the book by reiterating this point, and then discussing several ways researchers might design their simulations so they more arguably produce real evidence.

What are simulations for?
At the core, simulations are designed to generate _evidence_ for something.
We wish to use simulations to answer questions about the world: does this method generally work? Does it tend to work better than that one?
How large of a dataset do I need to answer this question as precisely as I wish?
Will outliers ruin my analysis?
We kicked off our book with a laundry list of simulation's many uses (@sec-introduction), and these questions will depend on the use we are after.

Some of the questions we ask are very specific: will the analysis work here?
Some are quite general: is this method robust to model misspecification?
For specific questions, we might care a lot about whether our simulation faithfully replicates certain aspects of our target context of interest.
In other words, the simulation needs to be _relevant_ to the situation being studied.
For the more general questions, we might not case so much about those details, but instead want to make sure our simulation covers as many different kinds of situations as possible.
This would be a concern about sufficient _generalizability_.

Some questions we might ask are about some sort of evaluative contest: is this method superior to that one?
These sorts of questions beg a kind of impartiality in the evaluation: we do not want our evidence to be rigged one way or the other.
In other words, we want our simulation to be _neutral_.
In other contexts, it might not be a pressing concern: if we are designing an analysis plan for a future empirical evaluation, then as long as that evaluation is conducted impartially, the selection of method is more a question of efficiency than bias.

Regardless of question, the arc of a simulation is to design, implement, and then analyze it.
The results of that analysis form a body of evidence that, ideally, can shine light on our question(s) of interest.
We evaluate our evidence to determine if our question is answered, or if more work needs be done.
We use our evidence to argue to others that our conclusions are correct, and should be trusted.

Of course, we want our simulations to not just be evidence, but be _good_ evidence.
To be good evidence, the results need to be answering the question posed, rather than some question that only appears to be the question posed.
The evidence also needs to be comprehensible: those digesting the evidence need to understand where it has come from, and be able to evaluate it.
This clarity is the concern of _transparency_.

Overall, _transparency_ is (we view) a universal concern: if you cannot understand what happened, you cannot evaluate whether it answers the question posed.
In this chapter we therefore first dive into how to make your reported results transparent, and then turn to the other three concerns from above: _relevance_, _generalizability_, and _neutrality_.
These concerns, while all generally important, can be more important for some uses of simulation than others.
For each of these virtues, we discuss how to create simulation evidence that is appropriate for the research agenda at hand.
We then close by discussing the specific case of writing simulation sections in statistical methodology papers.

<!--Now that we have all the tools in place we circle back to reflecting on those uses and, given the purpose of a simulation, what that says about whether the simulation is a successful one.

## Achieving Transparency {#sec-transparency}

Evidence that is not comprehensible is no evidence at all (regardless of what tends to happen in the literature, with overly technical and exhausting-to-decipher presentations all too often being given the benefit of the doubt).\index{transparency}

At root, transparency is built on clear writing and presentation.
It is also supported by providing reproducible code, so people can see exactly what you did, if they choose.
Transparency is mainly about how the work is communicated to an audience.
In the literature, there are many guides for clear reporting.
For example, @williams2024, building on the ADEMP framework [@morris2019UsingSimulationStudies], gives 11 principles to follow, including a handy table of where to put various results in a methods paper.

In the following we give our own list of high level principles to follow.


### Use figures, not tables

As we discussed extensively in prior chapters, use figures, not tables.
Figures allow you to show trends (as something goes up, something else goes down, and so forth).
Tables do not make trends apparent.
Making things apparent is a core value of transparency.

That said, including all your raw numbers in an excel table or csv file as supplemental material is also good for transparency.
You could also include these, or some of these, raw values in a supplementary write-up in the form of a classic table, possibly even with discussion, if you think people may be interested in exactly what those numbers are.


### Tell a coherent story

The best simulation sections should not be a list of very specific findings.
This, for example, is poor:

> In scenario A, method X had an RMSE\index{performance measures!RMSE} of 0.34, and method Y had an RMSE of 0.23, so Y was preferred, while in scenario B, method X's RMSE rose to 0.44 and Y rose to 0.52, which was higher. In scenario C, X's RMSE rose again to 0.55, higher than Y's 0.45, and in scenario D, X's RMSE was 0.40, lower than Y's 0.42.
  
This is better:

> Results were mixed: Method X outperformed Y in scenarios B and D, while Y outperformed X in scenarios A and C.
  
And even better:

> In Scenarios B and D, which had a nonlinear trend, method X outperformed Y, but Y was superior when the trend was linear.
  
In the discussion you then might have:

> Earlier we saw that method X outperformed Y when the trend was nonlinear, but Y outperformed X when the trend was linear. This is consistent with the fact that method X is designed to capture nonlinear trends: it has a stability cost (note the higher SEs on Table Q), but that cost is worth it if there is something to correct for. We generated our nonlinear trend based on our fit model to the applied example discussed in the next section; we therfore view the risk of increased bias in practical settings as quite real, and thus recommend using X over Y in practice, unless there is a strong reason to believe a linear trend.


Some people try to report all the results, without interpretation, and then have the discussion after.
Under this model, the reporting part can be extremely difficult to write, and extremely painful and boring to read.
Keep it short and refer to the tables and figures for the details.
Do not just list all those numbers without any contextualization.
Including everything does not, in the end, achieve transparency.

In fact, if you can get away with it, just present the figures and tables, and dive right into interpretation as you explain how to read those tables.
For example, continuing the running example from above:

> Table Q1 shows method X, with the bias correction, outperforms Y in the "nonlinear" scenarios, but Y outperforms when the trend is in fact linear. The higher RMSE in the linear scenarios is a stability cost (also note the higher SEs on Table Q2), but that cost is worth it if there is something to correct for. We generated ...

Give the reader your best understanding of why the proposed method works, when it works, how much it matters, and when one should or should not worry.

Select your visualizations to support your argument.
In the above, connect your linear scenarios with a line, and the non-linear ones with a different line, to make it easy to see the pattern.
Curate your visualizations to show the findings that matter, and put the remainder in the supplement for transparency.


### Give summaries, not details, in the main text

Extending the above, in the main text you might have summaries of your performance.
For example, in a large multifactor simulation of hundreds of scenarios, you might say

> Across the scenarios considered, the RMSE of method X ranged from 0.24 to 0.64. The other methods generally had higher RMSEs, ranging from 0.32 to 0.81. That said, in 15% of the scenarios explored, method X's RMSEs were more than 20% larger than the overall average, well beyond what could be explained by the Monte Carlo uncertainty.
  

### Keep the main text simple

Not everything should be in the main text.
Too much makes it hard for the reader to see the forest for the trees.
It is entirely appropriate to put secondary results---additional factor levels,
supplementary metrics, robustness checks---in an appendix or supplementary
materials.
What belongs in the main text are the figures that most directly
supports the central claim of the paper, presented as clearly and compactly as
possible.


### Report MCSEs, but do it concisely

If you cannot tell whether a displayed trend is potentially due to estimation error of the simulation itself, or something real, than the displayed trend can hardly be considered evidence for a claim.
In your paper, you should compute and report _Monte Carlo standard errors_ for
your key performance metrics.
All too often, researchers neglect to report MCSEs, making it hard to ascertain if their results are real, or noise.
Both @koehler2009AssessmentMonteCarlo and @williams2024, among others, conducted systematic reviews and found chronic under-reporting of any sense of simulation uncertainty.

Including simulation uncertainty can be tricky: including error bars from MCSEs on your plots, for example, can increase clutter substantially, which reduces transparency.
Instead consider putting the range of MCSEs in the caption of your plot.

Use the MCSEs as a guide for what findings are worth discussing.
Avoid reporting differences between methods that are smaller than the MCSEs you are calculating.
If arguing equivalence, say that your simulations show the methods are about the same, but could differ by about twice your MCSE (getting a true MCSE on the difference can be surprisingly tricky, as the estimated performance measures of different methods will be correlated).
Alternatively, use modeling on your experimental results to directly estimate differences.
See @sec-multilevel-meta-regression for further discussion.


### Report on error rates and convergence failures

@pawel2025's systematic review of nearly 500 studies found a chronic lack of reporting of when evaluated methods failed to provide a valid output due to failure to converge or having had an error.
Even fewer studies they reviewed discussed how such failures were handled.
At minimum, follow their core recommendation: always quantify and report missingness, even if none was observed.
If people do not know if your methods even converged, they cannot assess what your reported results mean in practice.
See @sec-warnings-and-errors for a bit more discussion of how to explore and report these concerns.


## Follow reporting guidelines or other conventional practices

Once one has generated all the results of a simulation, how should those results be reported?
@william2024 argues for _reporting guidelines_, \index{reporting guidelines} or standard practices that guide an author in what to do and where (for the specific case of writing academic papers).
As they put it, "Reporting guidelines enhance transparency by setting clear expectations for the inclusion and location of information, ensuring that readers can easily find and interpret the necessary details."

Of course, if writing simulations for some other purposes, such as power analyses for a grant application, or for communication with ones own research team, then these guidelines might differ.
The broader point remains, however: strive to report things clearly, and if there are conventions, following them can aid such clarity.



## Achieving Relevance {#sec-relevance}


For many of simulation's purposes, simulation results are a sort of "consumer product testing" for the statistical methods we are exploring.
Usually the first kind of testing are "clean" tests: tests using very simple or transparent data generating processes that do not attempt to capture the complexities of real data.
Clean tests are often easier to write, manipulate, and understand than more realistic simulations.
For example, we might write a simple parametric model data generation process with clear levers controlling the different aspects that might affect the performance of an estimator, even though we know the overall process is artificial.
Clean simulations can be used to push theory---we can experiment to gain an inclination of whether a novel approach to something is a good idea at all, or use a clean simulation to verify we are right about an intuition or derivation regarding how well an estimator might work.
Clean tests are often best-case (or at least optimistic) scenarios for when our estimator of interest will excel.
These can give a nominal upper bound on how well things could go.

Another kind of testing is "extreme testing" (the simulation equivalent of dropping things off buildings or driving over them with cars or whatever else).
Extreme tests are often also clean ones: with a clean and simple DGP, it is often easy to simply turn some of the DGP knobs to eleven to see how things break.
For simulation, extreme levels of a factor make understanding the role they play more clear.
Extreme contexts can also help lay bare the limits of our methods.

But from a "consumer product testing" standpoint, at least some of the tests conducted should be grounded in how consumers will actually use the product in real life.
Clean and extreme simulations cannot be the end of our journey.
In general, a researcher should work to ensure the sum total of their simulation evidence is _relevant_, meaning the simulations are capturing the important aspects of the target domain we are attempting to study.
The evidence should inform how things are likely to work out in practice.
A set of simulations only using unrealistic data generating processes is unlikely to accomplish this.
Unless the estimators being tested have truly universally stable properties, we will not learn much from a simulation if it is not relevant to the problem at hand.

Unfortunately, all too often, simulation sections of methods papers tend to remain in the world of the extreme, using DGPs so extreme that it is hard to image how they can provide anything other than a quick check of theory.
In reading papers, watch for exponential functions, extremely small amounts of noise relative to the variation of the covariates, or other features that make the DGP unrealistic.
And then avoid these practices in your own work.

So, after exploring the overly extreme or overly clean, how do we provide testing of the sorts of situations an eventual user of our methods might encounter in practice?
How can we make our simulations more relevant?

In the following subsections we go through a few strategies for making relevant simulations:

1.   Break symmetries and regularities.
2.   Pick simulation factors based on real data.
3.   Resample real data directly to get authentic distributions.
4.   Design a fully calibrated simulation.

Before we do, we talk a bit more about what relevance is, and how it can depend on context.

### But what is relevance?

Evidence being _relevant_ means that it is informing, in a legitimate way, the argument being made.
For example, if a simulation shows an estimator breaks, but the DGP is so unrealistic that any would agree it would never happen in practice, then the evidence of the estimator breaking is less relevant.
One could argue it is still somewhat relevant in that it shows the estimator _can_ break (a so-called existence proof), but this is less weighty than evidence of the estimator breaking in a simulation that is plausibly capturing what the real world looks like.

In the other direction, if an estimator is shown to be superior to another for a given simulation, that is evidence that the estimator _can_ be superior, but is not evidence that it is always superior.
In this case, an evidence body of a series of contexts that are all meaningfully different from one another, and where the estimator consistently out performs the other, would be meaningful and important.
In particular, the evidence would be evidence of a finding being _general_.
Whether the evidence is _relevant_ would be an assessment of whether the series of contexts are capturing the contexts we would generally see in practice: if all the contexts were implausible, or did not capture some aspect that could meaningfully drive the results, then the evidence, while in some sense general, would still not be relevant.

There are in effect two uses of the word "relevant."
The first is whether the evidence pertains to the question at hand.
The second is whether the evidence is rooted in a simulation that captures characteristics deemed to be important of the problem domain being studied.
This might be a very specific domain (our simulation should capture as close as possible the school district study we are planning) to broad (our simulation should capture the kinds of data social scientists will tend to use these methods on).
Regardless of the specificity, we use the word "relevant" primarily in this second sense.



### Break symmetries and regularities

In a series of famous causal inference papers [@lin2013agnostic; @freedman2008regression], researchers examined when linear regression adjustment of a randomized experiment (i.e., when controlling for baseline covariates in a randomized experiment) could cause problems.
Critically, if the treatment assignment is 50%, then the concerns that these researchers examined do not come into play, as asymmetries between the two groups get perfectly cancelled out.
That said, if the treatment proportion is more lopsided, then under some circumstances you can get bias and invalid standard errors, depending on other structures of the data.

Simulations can be used to explore these issues, but only if we break the symmetry of the 50% treatment assignment.
When designing simulations, it is worth looking for places of symmetry, because in those contexts estimators will often work better than they might otherwise, and other factors may not have as much of an effect on performance as anticipated.

Similarly, in recent work on best practices for analyzing multisite experiments [@miratrix2021applied], we identified how different estimators could be targeting different estimands.
In particular, some estimators target site-average treatment effects, some target person-average treatment effects, and some target a kind of precision-weighted blend of the two.
To see this play out in practice, our simulations needed the sizes of sites to vary, and also the proportion of treated within site to vary across sites.
If we had run simulations with equal site size or equal proportion treated, we would not see the broader behavior that separates the estimators considered.

Overall, it is important to make your data generation processes irregular.



### Pick simulation factors based on real data

To make a simulation relevant to a target context, use real data to inform choice of factor levels or other data generation features.
For example, in James's work on designing methods for meta-analysis, there is often a question of how big simulated sample sizes should be and how many different simulated outcomes per study there should be when generating sets of hypothetical studies to be included in hypothetical meta-analyses.
In one project, to make such simulations realistic, James obtained data from a set of past real meta-analyses and fit parametric models to these features, and then used the resulting parameter estimates as benchmarks for how large and how varied the simulated meta analyses should be.
<!-- LWM: James, can you put a cite here for reference? -->

When using values from the real world, we recommend not using the exact estimated values, but instead using them as a point of reference.
For instance, say we find that the distribution of study sizes fits a Poisson(63) pretty well.
We might then simulate study sizes using a Poisson with mean parameters of 40, 60, or 80 (where 40, 60, and 80 would be one factor in our multifactor experiment).


### Resample real data directly to get authentic distributions
\index{extand simulations}

You can use real data directly in your simulation if you want a simulation relevant to a specific, targeted context.
For example, say you need a population distribution for a slew of covariates.
Rather than using something artificial (such as a multivariate normal), you can pull population data on a collection of covariates from some administrative data and then use those data as your population distribution.
You then sample rows from your reference population (usually with replacement) to generate simulation samples.

An _extant simulation_ [@jaccard2021] is one where you generate complete datasets by resampling from a target dataset.
For extant simulations, the population parameters are then the estimates of the model on the full data, and the estimators try to recover those parameters on each sample.
See @jaccard2021 for a full treatment of running simulations in this way, along with some ideas of how to modify or tweak the resulting data to achieve different ends such as inducing null effects on some variables when needed.

The appeal of resampling is that whatever you resample will have distributions that are much more authentic than when generated via some parameteric model.
The resampled data automatically includes both continuous and categorical variables, and the variables will be skewed and correlated with each other in different ways that are more interesting than anything someone could make up (assuming the real data has these features).

@longUsingHeteroscedasticityConsistent2000 used an approach like this in their study of heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors.
They wanted to explore how well these standard errors worked in practice, with a focus on how high leverage points could undermine their effectiveness.
Leverage is purely a function of the covariate distribution, so they needed to have an authentic covariate distribution in order to properly explore this issue.
Generating realistic leverage is hard to do with a parametric model, so instead they used examples from real life to make the simulation more relevant.

### Build a semi-synthetic simulation

An extension of extant simulations (resampling data) is to resample the real data and then add an outcome model on top of that.
This two-step process is a form of **semi-synthetic**\index{semi-synthetic simulation} simulation, (the "semi" an acknowledgement of the hybrid approach), or **plasmode simulation**\index{plasmode simulation}, which has ties to electronic health records research.
These approaches are often used in causal inference work, where investigators attempt to determine which of the many observational study tools might work best, and when.
Causal inference simulations are particularly hard because even with real data in hand, there is no observed ground truth as to what the actual treatment effects are.
Everything must be estimated.

A key advantage of a semi-synthetic approach is that they can naturally adapt to rich contexts, such as electronic health records research, where covariate spaces can be extraordinarily high-dimensional, with complex dependence structures that a purely parametric
simulation could not plausibly reproduce [@franklin2014plasmode].
By simply bootstrapping the covariates from the raw data, all the dependencies are preserved.
A design question, if working in a causal inference framework, is then whether any treatment indicator should be included along with the covariates or generated independently; see, e.g., @shaw2025cautionary, who argue that sampling the treatment can cause estimators to appear spuriously biased in some cases.

Semi-synthetic approaches occupy the middle ground between purely synthetic
simulation (where every variable is fabricated from pre-specified distributions
and the data bear no necessary resemblance to any real population) and fully
empirical analysis (where ground truth treatment effects may be unobservable, making evaluation of an estimator difficult).

One canonical motivation for a semi-synthetic approach is the fundamental problem of causal inference: because we never observe counterfactual outcomes (e.g., the outcome we would have seen for a treated unit if it had not been treated) we cannot solely rely on the raw data if we are assessing a method's ability to estimate the "real" treatment effects.

A famous example of a semi-synthetic approach is the IHDP benchmark, in which @hill2011bayesian removed a subset of treated units from the Infant Health and Development Program randomized trial to introduce selection bias, and then replaced the observed
outcomes with simulated potential outcomes generated from a nonparametric
Bayesian model; this benchmark subsequently anchored a large fraction of the
machine-learning literature on heterogeneous treatment-effect estimation.
See, for example the Atlantic Causal Inference Conference data challenge, discussed in @dorie2019automated.
@gentzel2021how further systematized this approach, walking through different ways of generating data for simulation evaluation of causal inference methods.


### Build a calibrated simulation {#sec-calibrated-simulations}

Extending some of the prior ideas even further, one practice in increasing vogue is to generate _calibrated simulations_.
See @Kern2014calibrated for an example of a calibrated simulation in the context of generalizing experiments.
(Kern et al. is one of the earliest uses of the term "calibrated simulation," as far as we know.)

A calibrated simulation is one that is tailored to a specific applied context, with a DGP that is close to what we think the real world is like in that context.
Usually, this means we try to generate data that looks as much like a target dataset as possible, with the same covariate distributions and the same relationships between covariates and outcomes.
These simulations are not particularly general, but instead are designed to more narrowly inform how well things would work for the particular circumstance of focus.

Once we have a fully calibrated DGP, we can then modify it by adjusting sample sizes or other aspects to explore a space of DGPs that are all connected to this initially calibrated one.
This serves two purposes: first, we might be wrong about some of the details of our calibration, and exploring the space is a sensitivity check.
Second, we can then use our simulation to better understand what factors are important for good performance, just as with our other types of simulation discussed previously.
By exploring around our initially calibrated set we can thus still build more general evidence, but the evidence will always be anchored by our initial target.

We usually build a calibrated simulation out of existing data.
As discussed in the prior section, we might start with sampling from the covariate distribution of an actual dataset so that the distribution of covariates is authentic in how the covariates are distributed and, more importantly, how they co-relate.

Just putting a model on top of a real dataset does not necessarily achieve true calibration.
The relationship between our covariates and outcome would need to, even if it is model dependent, be realistic in order to truly assess how well the estimators work in practice.
It is very easy to accidentally put a very simple model in place for this final component, thus making a nominally calibrated simulation that is quite naive in, perhaps, the very way that counts.

One approach to get a more realistic model between covariates and outcomes is to fit a flexible model to the original data, and then use the model to predict outcomes from the covariates.
One would then generate residuals to add to the predictions, ideally in a way that preserves the heteroscedasticity and overall outcome distribution of the original data.
To illustrate this overall approach, in @sec-copula-case we provide a copula-based approach for generating synthetic outcomes closely coupled to the original data in a manner that allows control over how tightly coupled the covariates are to the outcome.
We do not say this is the only approach, but rather one of a large range of possibilities.

Clearly, calibration games can be fairly complex.
Calibrated simulations frequently do not lend themselves to a clear factor-based structure that have levers that change targeted aspects of the data generating process (although sometimes you can craft your approach to make such levers possible).
In exchange for this loss of clean structure, we end up with a simulation that might be more faithfully capturing aspects of a specific context, making our simulations more relevant to answering the narrower question of "how will things work here?" even if they are less relevant for answering the question of "how will things work generally?"









## Generalizability

The primary limitation of a simulation study is generalizability.
Read most narrowly, a simulation only tells you about what would happen in the worlds that are directly simulated.
Even if focused on a very narrow context of a single place, we still do not know if what we simulated actually matches, in all ways that are important, the single place being studied.

In response the adage of "if a single simulation is not convincing, use more of them," is one principle a researcher might take.
By conducting extensive multifactor simulations, once can explore a large space of possible data generating scenarios.
This is the core purpose of a multifactor simulations: If, across the full range of scenarios, a general story bears out, then perhaps that will be more convincing than a narrower range.
When we see a general finding over and over, or if we understand when we see it and when we do not, we have greater faith in how we might take the evidence of the simulation as a statement about the broader world.

Of course, no simulation is entirely generalizable---even an extensive full factorial design will entail many stylized assumptions and artificial constraints.
To withstand critiques about generalizability, simulations should be designed by aiming for comprehensiveness, including conditions that are relevant to real-life applications, and including conditions that allow for comparison to previous methodological work.
Although the result will surely fall short of perfect generalizability, we can still design simulations thoughtfully and, as best we can, avoid blatant limitations that a critic might identify as a basis for dismissing our findings.

So even for a simulation working to be general, those aspects that we chose not to vary need to be relevant, and those aspects we do vary need to be varied across ranges of values that make sense for our question being studied.
When taking on an argument for a general finding, a critic could, for example, claim that some aspect of the DGP that is not varying is the real culprit.
If this aspect is unrealistic, then the findings, across the board, are then less relevant, and the evidence for the overall claim is made weak.

Generalzability and relevance work together; they are not actually on opposite ends of a spectrum.
That said, it is often easier to vary and explore a range of scenarios with a more classic multifactor simulation of a model-based DGP than a carefully crafted simulation calibrated to a specific, narrow context.
And when doing this work, pick the factors one varies with care, and pick factors in anticipation of reviewer critique.



## Neutrality {#sec-neutrality}


As put by Boulesteix and others, in statistical methodology, the famous "publish or perish" adage could be reframed as "publish new methods or perish" [@boulesteix2017necessity].
This pressure in turn arguably creates strong incentives for researchers to find simulations that make their contributions appear meaningful, and thus we should, a priori, trust a simulation showing a new method's dominance with some skepticism.
It also means those wishing to _use_ a method for actual analysis face a daunting number of choices as to what method might be best.
One solution are carefully done comparative simulations that lay out when a method is better than another, to help guide practice.
In other words, such simulations (if well done) are important and we need more of them!

The above quoted Boulesteix letter builds on the authors prior work [@boulesteix2013Plea] that proposes a framework for "neutrality" in comparative simulation evaluations.
After a systematic review establishing that, indeed, articles where authors are developing a method tend to find that method is superior, while articles that are more comparison focused tend to find more mixed results, they build a framework for what might constitute neutrality:

A. The main focus of the article is the comparison itself (and _not_ the development of a novel method).
B. The authors themselves are reasonably neutral. As put in their paper, "an author who has published an article on a new method six months before is likely to be less neutral than an author who has often used several of the considered methods for statistical consulting."
C. The simulation design (evaluation criteria, methods, data sets used) should be well motivated. (In their paper, Section 4 unpacks how this might be done.)

Pushing on why simulation evidence is often not to be trusted, @pawel2023 provide a taxonomy of "QRPs," or Questionable Research Practices, that can result in simulations that seem to find things that are not true.
These QRPs (including not justifying number of simulations, not reporting MCSEs, dropping comparison methods or scenarios from reporting, or choosing performance metrics strategically) can appear anywhere in the pipeline---design, execution, or reporting---of a simulation's creation.
To prove their point, in their paper they demonstrate generating "evidence" for the superiority of a novel prediction method that has no actual benefit, using their QRPs.\index{Questionable Research Practices}

The three principles of Boulesteix and colleagues and the danger of QRPs should be kept in mind regardless of ones purpose for simulation.
In particular, even if developing a method, finding the edges where the method fails is a service to the field, and strengthens the plausibility of claims regarding when the method is more successful.
Researchers should, at minimum, conduct simulations in a manner to prevent _oneself_ from being deceived---it is all to easy to rationalize via post-hoc reasoning unless one puts checks and balances for oneself in place.
As an extreme stance on this, @siepe2024SimulationStudiesMethodological argue for pre-analysis plans, which could help keep researcher bias in check; while true, we find this to be difficult to implement in practice, although @pawel2023 does offer some suggestions on how to be more flexible, yet clear, with such an approach.\index{pre-analysis plans}
See our discussion in @experimental-design-conclusion.

We next provide a series of principles to encourage neutrality and promote the plausibility, and thus the quality of the final evidence, of ones work.


### Avoid selective reporting

Simulations are particularly susceptible to selective reporting, one of the sins identified by @pawel2023.
The combination of degrees of freedom available to the researcher and the pressure
to present results favorably creates a real risk of findings that do not paint an accurate picture.

There are three ways to defend against selective reporting.

The first is advanced planning.\index{advanced planning}
Before running your main set of simulations, think through the full set of factors you will vary
and commit to a range of levels for each.
If you deviate from this plan---because a factor turned out not to matter, or
because a computational constraint forced a change---be transparent about why.
Full factorial designs, with all combinations of all levels, are preferable to
hand-selected sets of scenarios precisely because they leave less room for
post-hoc selection.

The second is code sharing.\index{code sharing}
Code sharing is increasingly expected in many fields, and for simulation studies
it is particularly valuable.
Sharing the simulation code allows readers to verify results, extend the simulation
to additional conditions, or reproduce your findings if they are skeptical.
Beyond serving the field, code sharing also disciplines the researcher: knowing that others
could read and run the code tends to make one more careful and more honest.
In practice, this means keeping simulation code clean and well-documented, something
that the software engineering practices discussed earlier in this book will help
facilitate.

The third is to find contexts where your methods fail.
If you present simulations that include boundaries where your methods fail, then you are giving a more complex picture of the landscape of performance.
You also gain credibility: by showing areas where things fall apart, you are signaling that you are not just cherry picking favorable results.


### Be fair with the selection of performance measures
\index{performance measures}

The choice of what to measure in a simulation is not neutral.
Different metrics emphasize different aspects of performance, and a method that
looks good on one metric can look bad on another.
Bias measures systematic error; variance measures precision; mean squared error
combines them.
Coverage of confidence intervals assesses the full inferential pipeline.
Type I error rate assesses validity of tests under the null.
Power assesses sensitivity.
The computational time a method takes is sometimes also relevant.

Depending on the research questions being asked, some of these matter more than others.
If you are proposing a new estimator meant to correct a bias problem, bias is
obviously central.
If you are proposing a new test for a hypothesis where existing tests are known to
be anti-conservative, Type I error rate is central.
Think carefully about which metrics are directly relevant to the specific claim your
paper is making, and report those prominently.
Do not, of course, report only favorable metrics.
Do report a more full range of metrics in your appendix, if you are only presenting a few in the main paper.

Do not focus overly narrowly on your primary metric, however.
For example, methods that controls bias tightly can often have much larger variances.
If you are introducing a new method that controls bias, you should first show bias reduction, but also show that your method achieves a favorable bias-variance trade-off.



### Use simulation DGPs from prior literature. 

If a relevant prior paper uses a simulation to make a case, one approach is to replicate that simulation, adding in the new estimator one wants to evaluate.
In effect, use previously published simulations to beat them at their own game.
Using an established DGP makes it (more) clear that you are not fishing: you are using something that already exists in the literature as a published benchmark.
By constraining oneself to published simulations, one has less wiggle room to cherry pick a data generating process that works the way you want.
Indeed, such a benchmarking approach is often taken in the machine learning literature, where different canonical datasets are used to benchmark the performance of new methods.



### The tension between impartiality and learning


@white2023HowCheckSimulation gives a variety of high-level advice regarding what to do when one's simulation results are confusing (e.g., check if you have correctly implemented one versus two sided tests if rejection rates or power is surprising).
Confusing results will happen a lot, and when you get them, it will often be hard to tell if that is because you are learning something about your methods, or you are learning something about errors in your code.

Iteratively exploring confusing results, and then repairing your simulation, is generally good practice, but it also can lead to fishing.
As discussed in @sec-neutrality and @experimental-design-conclusion, other researchers (e.g., @pawel2023 and @siepe2024SimulationStudiesMethodological) have raised valid concerns about "simulations being doomed to succeed," which is a function of tinkering with a simulation until it behaves as you believe it should.
There is a real tension between getting it right, and deceiving oneself.

One simple practice is to keep a log of the overall process, and before running any large simulation, writing a small memo predicting what you expect to see.
White et al. provide some further advice, such as checking the Monte Carlo error---sometimes a surprising result is actually just due to random chance!
Checking to make sure the results are real (First MCSEs, and then looking for errors in implementation) is always the first step one should take.







## Simulation sections in methods papers

Simulations, as we have argued, have many uses, and appear in many places.
One of the most prevalent is the simulation section of a statistical methods paper.
But what are simultions in this world trying to accomplish?
And, given what they are trying to accomplish, how should they be done?

In what follows, we discuss several related goals that simulations in
methods papers should serve, along with practical guidance on how to accomplish
each of them.
Also see @william2024, for, in the context of writing a simulation study up in an academic paper, further discussion and guidance as to what reporting goes where.

<!--
We then give some advice on navigating the many design decisions of a simulation, and conclude with some guiding principles for achieving these ends.


In this section, we make a case for what the simulation evidence in a methods paper should look like, and outline several principles to consider if you are writing up, or reviewing, such a section.
-->

### What is the simulation section for?

Ideally, a simulation study in a methods paper is not decoration but instead evidence for an overall argument.
These arguments can be pointed (the researcher has an agenda to prove) or more exploratory (the researcher is trying to learn something).
Which kind of argument is being conducted depends on what kind of methods paper is being written.

Broadly speaking, there are a few kinds of methods papers that involve simulation.
Likely the most common is a "new method" paper, where the researchers propose some novel approach, have some (mathematical) theory arguing for its utility, have a simulation to justify or illustrate the argument, and finally an applied example to demonstrate the method's use.
For these papers, the simulation is often presented as evidence that "our proposed method is an improvement over whatever else is out there."

<!--The simulation evidence is then the empirical case for whatever claim is being made.-->

A second type of methods paper is a "simulation paper," where the researchers are specifically using simulation to evaluate some set of research questions, usually in the context of finite performance when we only have asymptotic theoretical results.
For example, a paper might be tackling a research question such as, "how often will these procedures identify the right number of latent groups?"
In one example from Luke's work [@miratrix2021applied], he used simulation to assess whether differences in a set of average treatment effect estimates could be driven by cross-site treatment variation in multisite trials; the paper primarily focused on a series of empirical data evaluations, but used simulation to understand possible drivers for differences in apparent empirical performance.

One version of these evaluative papers are papers attempting to offer guidance as to which method, of a set of methods, to use in practice.
Here there is not necessarily a new method being sold, but instead the research question is 
"which of a set of methods is most appropriate for our given context of interest?"
Now the simulation results are evidence to help adjudicate which options are most promising, and when.
(Ideally the "context of interest" part of the research question is explicit--papers attempting to answer "which method is best" are generally doomed due to all methods having different weaknesses; any simulation that finds a unilateral winner is likely not _general_ enough.)

Regardless of type, the simulation evidence is only good insofar as it is appropriately relevant, general, and, especially in the context of a horse race of methods, neutral.

All if this said, we believe the simulation section is not just about the apparent question of "which method is best," but actually serves (or should serve) to answer a range of questions that we delineate below.


### Several overlooked purposes for simulation in methods papers

Simulation is for more than just horse-racing.
Here are four reasons for a simulation section that have nothing to do with method comparison.
Especially considering anyone reading a simulation section arguing for a new method's superiority should take the entire section with a large grain of salt due to complete lack of neutrality, we recommend writing papers to achieve these ends in addition to any selling of methods one might do.


#### Increase belief in the theory

We generally hope that a mathematical theorem in a paper is correct, but few of us will spend the time carefully reading any accompanying proof or derivation to ensure this is so.
In fact, many papers have these derivations in a supplement, and often they are cut down versions of the original proofs, without providing many of the intermediate steps.

Simulation can provide a sanity check and reassurance in this case.
One might even say that the most basic job of a simulation is to verify that the theory behind a method actually works.
Such a "sanity check" simulation is often a simple one.
A clean, stylized data generating process with the key structural features the
theory assumes---perhaps independent errors, a specific parametric form for the
outcome, or a particular covariate distribution---is entirely appropriate here.
The goal is not to show that the method works in a realistic context; it is to show
that the theory does what it says it does.
For example, if your theory says the estimator has a bias that diminishes at rate $1/n$, you should see this as a linear relationship of bias vs. $n$ on a log scale.


For a theory check type of simulation, one useful practice is to verify not just that the
point estimates look right, but also that the uncertainty quantification is correct.
Coverage of nominal 95% confidence intervals is a particularly demanding test:
it requires both that the point estimate be close to unbiased and the standard error be well estimated.
Showing close-to-nominal coverage in a clean setting can be a quite meaningful form of theoretical verification.


#### Increase a paper's readibility

Methods papers can be extremely technical, and the theory can be difficult to understand.
If the notation is not well laid out (which in many cases it is not), even deciphering what a theorem is saying, or what an estimator actually is, can be difficult.
The simulation section often has to get down to brass tacks, laying out the problem cleanly.
Thus simulations can be an accessible entry point into a paper, providing some concrete examples of the context the estimators were designed for, what assumptions the estimators depend on, and so forth.

While we advocate making the an entire paper readable, we also note that a good simulation can help add clarity to your overall project.
Clean simulations of this type are also useful for illustrating _how_ the method works.


#### Demonstrate finite-sample relevance

Most statistical theory is asymptotic: as $n \to \infty$, the
estimator is consistent; as the number of studies grows, the coverage of a confidence
interval approaches 95%; as the sample size grows, some test statistic converges to
a chi-squared distribution.
Such asymptotic results might say little about whether the method works at the sample sizes anyone would actually encounter.
Simulations, on the other hand, can show that at some reasonable $n$, things are in fact close to what theory promises (for at least the contexts explored).
For an alarming example of such perils of "asymptopia," @kang2018inference examines weak instruments for Instrumental Variable analysis.
Even though asymptotic IV estimators guarantee 95% coverage _eventually_, Kang et al. find coverage below 50%!

Simulation, not (in general) theory, can show that the method works---
or can characterize how well it works---in the finite-sample conditions that are
realistic for the problem.
If you have derived a new estimator and proved it is consistent and asymptotically
normal, a simulation showing that at $n = 500$ the bias is small, the sampling
distribution is approximately normal, and the confidence intervals achieve close to
nominal coverage could be reassuring to readers in a way that the asymptotic proof alone might not be.
Readers are (rightly) skeptical of novel methods, and seeing the theory confirmed in a clean, interpretable simulation builds trust.

Finite-sample performance heavily depends on a well-crafted multi-factor structure.
Finite-sample performance depends on more than just $n$.
It depends on signal-to-noise ratios, covariate distributions, the complexity of
the true outcome model, the degree of model misspecification, and a host of
other features.
A convincing finite-sample simulation should vary these features systematically,
using levels that span the realistic range of what practitioners in the domain
are likely to encounter.
A finite-sample simulation that is overly clean will not provide evidence relevant to assessing finite sample performance in practice.

Building a truly representative multi-factor simulation does put a burden on the researcher to understand their domain.
What are typical sample sizes in the field?
What kinds of covariate structures are common?
How much model misspecification should one worry about?
The simulation factors you choose, and the levels you assign to them, are an
implicit argument about what a domain looks like.



#### Motivate and contextualize the subsequent applied analysis

A methods paper often includes an applied data analysis, usually to show that the
methods work on real data and to make an appeal that the methods designed are not completely useless or irrelevant.
Simulations can play a supporting role here.
If your applied analysis shows that methods A and B gave different answers, then you might need your simulation section to make the case that we should believe A and not B.

Such a case can be best built via what one might call a _domain-calibrated simulation_, distinct from the multifactor simulation.
Where the multifactor simulation explores many conditions to establish (ideally) general properties, a domain-calibrated simulation would be specifically designed to mimic the applied dataset in the paper.
It is built using the methods discussed above in @sec-relevance: the covariate distribution might be drawn from the actual data, the outcome model might be fit to the actual data, and key features of the real setting (sample size, proportion treated, etc.) would all be matched.

The purpose of this calibrated simulation is not to add statistical generality---it may add very little---but to argue that, in a context that looks a lot like the problem we care about, we should prefer one method over another.
This is especially true if the multifactor simulation shows that in some cases we might prefer the other method, or if in some cases there is no real difference between the two.

A natural structure for a methods paper, then, is to present the multifactor
simulation first to establish a general story, and then follow it with a
calibrated simulation tied to the applied data.


### What to present in a methods paper

Following the principles in @sec-transparency and somewhat following @william2024, we suggest putting most of the simulation write up in a supplemental appendix.
The main paper should be clear on the factors considered, give a sense of the data generation process used, and then have results in the form of a few well-chosen figures.
In most cases any tables can be relegated elsewhere.

@morris2019UsingSimulationStudies proposed a framework for the design of a simulation that they named "ADEMP," standing for Aim (A), Data-generating mechanism (D), Methods (M), Estimand (E), and Performance measures (P).
Each of these should be clearly reported in the main paper, at least at a high level.
In particular, giving _reasons_ for the DGP used or performance measures used can clarify the aims of the simulation and also make the argument for how the evidence matters more salient.
At the very least, the technical details implied by the above list should be reported at least in the supplements.

This reasonable floor on practice is regularly not achieved.
Surprisingly, even the first component, "Aim," is rarely reported: @william2024 found only "9% of the articles in our survey did not explicitly specify their aims" (pg 1931).
Further, they found 25% of studies reviewed did not explain or justify their choice of data-generation mechanism.
Arguably worse, their survey found only 11% of studies failed to clearly report the used performance measures either.
Without understanding how simulated data were generated or what metric of success was used, or why it was chosen, any presented evidence is hard to parse or believe.

Reporting is not just limited to a writeup of the simulation process and findings.
Following principles of transparency, there is no reason to not include code, including the code to analyze the results of the simulation itself.
@william2024 found nearly a third of studies evaluated did not bother to make these resources available.
Do not be such a bad actor!

For a methods paper, simulations should generally serve at least three
purposes: verifying that the theory is correct in clean conditions, demonstrating
that the method works in finite samples at realistic scales for the domain, and
motivating the applied analysis by showing how the method performs in a context
that resembles the real application.
Make the purposes of your simulation clear.

Simulation studies should use performance metrics that are directly relevant to the paper's central
claims, report enough replications to make the results trustworthy, and be
presented in a way that tells a coherent story rather than merely exhausting the reader with numbers and details.
Getting all of this right is not easy, but it is what separates a simulation study
that genuinely advances knowledge from one that merely fills space between the theory
section and the data analysis.

Simulations generally have a bad reputation, and that is unfortunately deserved.
When reading methods papers, keep an eye out for extreme simulations that have no connection to reality, simulations that only report on one metric, leaving other ones unstated, and reported measures where it is impossible to tell if a difference is substantively meaningful or not.
These examples are all too easy to find.
Please do not increase the pool, in this regard.


  

## Concluding thoughts

Simulations are a way of generating evidence of research claims.
Good research using good simulations, therefore, will make those claims explicit and then clearly explain how the simulation provides evidence that relevant and sufficiently general to answer the posed questions.
The presentation should be sufficiently transparent so that the claims can be evaluated and the evidence understood and weighed.
Ideally, as part of this, sufficient steps can be taken to assuage any concerns about too much researcher bias in the process: neutrality is a value to be considered especially strongly when reading evidence arguing for the superiority of one approach over another.

Just as the simulation itself should be tailored to the problems at hand, the presentation of the simulation should be tailored to the context at hand.
A lot of this is art, but we believe that adhering primarily to the principles of transparency---usually by using direct language and clear plots---most of these goals will almost directly be achieved.






## Addendum Case study: using copulas to generate calibrated data {#sec-copula-case}
\index{copula}

<!-- LWM: I stole from my blog post and cut it down a bit.  But this might be overly specialized.  I wanted to make the calibrated discussion a bit more explicit above.  But perhaps we should cut? -->

<!-- LWM: Should this all be pushed to Part V? or should it stay here? -->


In this section, we borrow from a blog post^[See (https://cares-blog.gse.harvard.edu/post/copulas-for-simulation/)] to illustrate how to use copulas to generate data that is very calibrated to a target dataset.
In this example, we will generate new observations $(X, Y)$, where $X$ is a vector of covariates (some continuous, some categorical) and $Y$ is a continuous outcome of an arbitrary distribution as described by a target dataset.

A copula is a mathematical device that is used to describe a multivariate distribution in terms of its marginals and the correlation structure between them, and we used it to generate new $Y_i$ values based on the $X_i$ in a way that maintained the same marginal distributions for all variables as the empirical dataset.

We found the copula to have several benefits.
First, the copula approach can give a different $Y$ for a given $X$.
By contrast, simply bootstrapping our empirical data (a common way to generate synthetic data that looks like an empirical target) would not achieve this.
Second, we could control the tightness of the coupling between $X$ and $Y$, while maintaining a fairly complex and nonlinear relationship between $X$ and $Y$, and while maintaining possible heteroskedasticity found in the initial dataset.


```{r setup_sim_evidence, include=FALSE}

N = 3000
Sigma_X = diag( c(1,2,3) ) + 1
Sigma_X[1,2] = Sigma_X[2,1] = -0.8
Sigma_X

#I use some fake data generated with this code:

X = mvrnorm( 2*N, mu=c(1,2,3), Sigma = Sigma_X)
colnames(X) = paste0( "X", 1:ncol(X) )

  dat <- X |> as_tibble() |>
    mutate( X4 = X1 + rnorm( n() ),
            Y = (1 * X1^2 + 2 * X1*X2 + exp(X3 / 2 ) + rnorm(2*N, sd=4))^2,
            Y = pmin( Y, quantile( Y, 0.95 ) ),
            X1 = round( 2*X1 ),
            X2 = 0 + ( X2 >= 0.5 ) )
  
  dat$Y[ dat$Y > 300 & dat$Y < 800 ] = 550

```

```{r, include=FALSE}
new_data = dat[1:N,]
new_data <- rename( new_data,
                    trueY = Y )
dat = dat[(N+1):(2*N),]

#plot(dat)
```

To illustrate, we will use a (fake) dataset with four covariates, X1, X2, X3, and X4, and an outcome, Y.
Here are a few rows of this "empirical" data that we are trying to match:

```{r, echo=FALSE}
dat |> 
  slice_tail( n = 5 ) |>
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
```

Our outcome in this case is a bit funky:

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 2.5

qplot( dat$Y, bins = 30 )
```

The covariates have a correlation structure with themselves and also Y.
Here are the pairwise correlations on the raw values:

```{r}
print( round( cor( dat ), digits = 2 ) )
```

We want to generate synthetic data that captures the correlation structure of our empirical data along with the marginal distributions of each covariate and outcome.
We will do this via the following steps:

**Steps for making data with a copula:**

1. Predict $Y$ given the full set of covariates $X$ using a machine learner.
2. Tie $\hat{Y}_i$ and $Y_i$ together with a copula.
3. Generate new $X$s (in our case, via the bootstrap).
4. Generate a predicted $\hat{Y}_i$ for each $X_i$ using the machine learner.
5. Generate the final, observed, $Y_i$ using our copula.

### Step 1. Predict the outcome given the covariates

We can use some machine learning model to make predictions of $Y$ given $X$.
Here we use a random forest:

```{r}
library(randomForest) 
mod <- randomForest( Y ~ ., 
                     data=dat,
                     ntree = 200 )
dat$Y_hat = predict( mod )
```

Our predictive model for $Y$ can be anything we want: we are just trying to get some predicted $Y$ that is appropriately tied to the $X$.

Our predictions will be under dispersed and not natural in appearance.
For starters, the standard deviation of the $\hat{Y}$ will be less than the original $Y$, because our predictions are only getting at the structural aspects, not the residual noise:

```{r}
tibble( sd_Yhat = sd( dat$Y_hat ),
        sd_Y = sd( dat$Y ),
        cor = cor( dat$Y_hat, dat$Y ) ) |>
  knitr::kable( digits = c(1,1,2) )
```

Our synthetic $Y$ values will need to be "noised up" so they look more natural.
We also want them to match the empirical distribution of our original data.


### Step 2. Tie $\hat{Y}$ to $Y$ with a copula

The first step of the copula approach is to make a function that converts empirical data to normalized $z$-scores based on their percentile rank, as we will be doing all our data generation in "normal $z$-score space."
In other words, we take a value, calculate its percentile, and then calculate what $z$-score that percentile would have, if the value came from a standard normal distribution.

Here is a function to do this:
```{r}
convert_to_z <- function( Y ) {
  K = length(Y)
  r_Y <- rank( Y, ties.method = "random" )/K - 1/(2*K)
  z <- qnorm( r_Y )
  z
}
```
We calculate percentiles by ranking the values, and then taking the midpoint of each rank.
If we had 20 values, for example, we would then have percentiles of 5%, 15%, ..., 95%.
(We can't have 0 or 100% since this will turn into Infinity when converting to a $z$-score.)

Using our function, we convert both our $Y$ and predicted $Y$ to these normal $z$-scores:
```{r, messages=FALSE}
#| code-fold: true
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
#| out-width: 80%

z_Y = convert_to_z( dat$Y )
z_Yhat = convert_to_z( dat$Y_hat )

qplot( z_Y, z_Yhat, asp = 1, alpha=0.05 ) +
  geom_abline( slope=1, intercept=0, col="red" ) +
  labs( 
    title = "z-scores of Y vs predicted Y",
    x = expression(z[Y]),
    y = expression(z[hat(Y)])
  ) +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme( legend.position = "none" )
```

Note how the $z$-scores have smoothed our Y distribution due to the random ties, breaking up our spikes of identical values.
We can then see how coupled the predicted and actual are:

```{r}
stats <- tibble( 
  rho = cor( z_Y, z_Yhat ),
  sd_Y = sd( z_Y ),
  sd_Yhat = sd( z_Yhat ) )
stats
```

### Step 3. Get some new Xs

So far we are just modeling relationship in our original data.
We next set the stage for generating a new dataset.
We start with making more $X$ values.
A simple trick is to simply bootstrap the data, keeping the $X$ only.
We might, for example, generate a new dataset of 500 observations like so:

```{r}
nd = dat |>
  dplyr::select( starts_with("X") ) |>
  slice_sample( n = 500, replace = TRUE )
```

If we don't want exact duplicates of the vectors of $X$ values in our data, we can use other methods such as the `synthpop` package, which generates data based on a series of conditional distributions.

So we can check our work later, we are instead going to cheat and use a dataset, `new_data` that is generated from the same DGP as our original fake data.
It looks like so:

```{r, echo=FALSE}
new_data
```

To be very specific, `trueY` would not normally be in our data at this point; we have it here so we can compare our generated Y to the true Y to see how well our DGP is working.
In practice, we would not be able to do this: we would need to generate new $X$ like shown above.


### Step 4. Generate a predicted $\hat{Y}_i$ for each $X_i$ using the machine learner.

This step is quite easy:

```{r}
new_data$Yhat = predict( mod, newdata = new_data )
```

Done!

### Step 5. Generate the final, observed, $Y_i$ using a copula that ties $\hat{Y}_i$ to $Y_i$.

Now we generate our new $Y$ by converting our predictions (the Yhat) to the new $Y$ via the copula.
We are bascially using the same pieces that are in the $z$-score function, above.

We first generate the percentiles the Y-hats represent:
```{r}
K = nrow(new_data)
new_data$r_Yhat = rank( new_data$Yhat ) / K - 1/(2*K)
summary( new_data$r_Yhat )
```

We then convert the percentiles to the $z$-scores they represent:
```{r}
new_data$z_Yhat = qnorm( new_data$r_Yhat )
summary( new_data$z_Yhat )
```

We next use a formula for the conditional distribution of a normal variable given the other variable, namely, if $X_1, X_2$ both have unit variance and mean zero, we use
$$X_2 | X_1 = a \sim N( \rho a, 1 - \rho^2 ) .$$
With this formula, we generate $Y$ as so:

```{r}
rho = cor( z_Y, z_Yhat ) # from our empirical
new_data$z_Y = rnorm( K, 
                      mean = rho * new_data$z_Yhat, 
                      sd = sqrt( 1-rho^2 ) )
```

Now, finally, for each observation in z-space, we figure out what rank it would correspond to in our empirical distribution, and then take that empirical data point as the value:

```{r}
empDist = sort(dat$Y)
K = length(empDist)
new_data$r_Y = ceiling( pnorm( new_data$z_Y ) * K )
new_data$Y = empDist[ new_data$r_Y ]
```

And we are done!

### Assessing the copula's success

Let us next see how the distribution of our generated $Y$ to the true $Y$ from the real DGP:

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3

dtL <- 
  new_data |>
  pivot_longer( 
    cols = c( Y, Yhat, trueY ), 
    names_to = "kind", values_to = "Y" 
  )

ggplot( dtL, aes( Y ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ kind, nrow= 1 ) +
  geom_histogram( alpha=0.5, binwidth = 100 )
```
`trueY` and $Y$ are very close!  Note the Yhat is quite different, by contrast.

We further check our process by looking at how closely the correlations of our new Y with the Xs match the correlations of the true Y and the Xs:

```{r, echo=FALSE}
cor( new_data[ c( "X1","X2", "X3", "X4", "Yhat", "Y", "trueY" ) ] ) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column( "Variable" ) |>
  dplyr::select( Variable, Y, trueY ) |>
  dplyr::filter( !(Variable %in% c( "Yhat", "Y", "trueY" )) ) |>
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
```
Our new Y roughly looks like the true Y, with respect to the correlation with the Xs.
We gave our copula approach a hard test here--simpler covariate relationships will be better captured.
That said, this doesn't seem that bad.

<!--In our $z$-space we match by design; it is the transform that is distorting our relationship:
```{r, eval=FALSE}
new_data$z_trueY = convert_to_z(new_data$trueY)
cor( new_data[ c( "z_Yhat", "z_Y", "z_trueY" ) ] ) |>
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
```
-->


### Building a multifactor simulation from our calibrated DGP

In the above, we made a DGP that mimics, as closely as we can, the empirical data we are targeting.
In an actual simulation, however, we would generally want to manipulate different aspects of our DGP to explore how different methods might function.

We offer some examples of how to do this for this context.

First, we can directly set `rho` to control how tightly coupled the outcome is to the covariates.
If `rho` is 0, then our outcome distribution will be exactly the same, but there would be no connection between it and the covariates.
For `rho` of 1, the outcome would be perfectly predicted by the predicted outcome, which is a function of the covariates.
The strength of the connection between $X$ and $Y$ is maximized.


Second, we can easily control sample size by generating larger or smaller datasets of $X$ and then generating $Y$ from those $X$.

Third, we can drop some of our $X$s by simply not including them in the prediction model, thus making them noise variables.
We may still end up with relationships between a dropped $X$ and $Y$ due to the dropped $X$'s correlation structure with other $X$s that are tied to $Y$.
